title: The city of nine gates
hook: a stranger in a Varanasi lane asks Shankara which self should move aside, and the Gita explains the answer
carry: the same self sits in every body

segments.voice: Yesterday, two paths, renouncing and acting, and a lotus leaf that lives in the water without getting wet. Both reach the goal. Today, a city.
screen: `RENOUNCE OR ACT — BOTH REACH THE GOAL.`

segments.voice: Varanasi, on the river Ganga, more than a thousand years ago. The teacher Shankara is walking by the river with his students. In a narrow lane, a man comes the other way with four dogs: a man the society of that day treated as untouchable. Shankara tells him: move aside. The man doesn't move. He asks a question instead. Which should move away from which? This body, made of food, from that body, made of food? Or the self in me from the self in you, when it's the same self? Shankara stops. And he bows.
screen: `VARANASI, A NARROW LANE.` → `MOVE ASIDE, SOMEONE SAYS.` → `WHICH SELF SHOULD MOVE?`

segments.voice: That's a story told about Shankara; in many tellings the stranger was Shiva himself. Shankara answered in verse: whoever truly sees this, born outcaste or born a priest, is my teacher. The idea is the Gita's, chapter five. Verse thirteen: the one who lives in the body sits at ease in the city of nine gates. The nine gates are the body's openings: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, the mouth, and the two openings for waste. And who lives in the city? An old word-play hears purusha, the person, as the one who dwells in the pura, the city. Hindus call that dweller the atman: the self, the real you. Many teachers, Shankara among them, say it is one with Brahman, God in everything. The doing, verse fourteen says, is nature doing what nature does. Then verse eighteen, the verse the man in the lane was living: the wise look with the same eye at a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a person society shuns. Because the same one is seated in every city. It's why many Hindus greet with folded hands, namaste, I bow to you, and many explain it as a bow to the divine in you. Today it meets the people you look past: the person cleaning the office, the kid nobody sits with. The same self sits there.
screen: `THE STRANGER IN THE LANE.` · `NINE GATES: EYES, EARS, NOSTRILS, MOUTH…` · `THE ATMAN, SEATED WITHIN.` · `THE SAME EYE ON EVERY BEING.` · then, large: `THE SAME SELF IN EVERY BODY.`

segments.voice: Visit the gates one at a time: your eyes, noticing light; your ears, the nearest sound, then the farthest; your nostrils, the cool air coming in. You don't have to close any gate. Notice that something in the middle is noticing. Then bring to mind one person you passed today without really seeing, and silently, hands folded if you like, say namaste to the one seated in them.
Purusha. The person, the one who dwells in the city. Hindus call that dweller the atman, the self: seated at ease behind the nine gates, and the same in every body.
Carry this: the same self sits in every body. The same eye for the priest, the dog, and the man in the lane. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 176 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE PEACE THAT DOESN'T END.`

howItsDone: Hindus greet with folded hands and namaste (literally 'I bow to you'), which many explain as a bow to the self or the divine in the other; in meditation, some draw attention inward from the senses, the 'gates' of Gita 5.13.

fork.setup: a man with four dogs won't move aside for a great teacher. by verse 18, how do the wise see him?
options: below the teacher, so he should move.
with the same eye: the same self is in both.
above the teacher, because he's humble.
fork.reveal: with the same eye: sama-darshinah. the same atman is seated in every body, so Shankara bowed.

original.note: Sanskrit: nava-dvare pure, 'in the city of nine gates'. nava, nine; dvara, door; pura, city.

trapdoor: what you thought: namaste is just a polite hello.
what it means: a bow to the one seated in the other's body, the same self, the atman, that sits in yours.

what a scholar hears: the body as a city (pura) with gates also appears in the Upanishads; an old word-play hears purusha as the one dwelling in the pura; the lane story frames five short verses traditionally credited to Shankara.
recall: an offering, a gift given back

chat.says: Sam was over and saw nani do namaste to the guy fixing our sink, the exact same way she does to the pandit at the mandir 🙏 Sam asked if that's a rule. wait, why does she do it to EVERYONE?
options: the gita says the wise see a priest, a cow, a dog, anyone, with the same eye, bc the same self sits in every body. her namaste bows to that.

chat.meaning: Gita 5.18: the wise see every being with the same eye, because the same self, the atman, is seated in every body. Many Hindus explain namaste as a bow to that self in the other.

tie.story: In a Varanasi lane, a man told to move aside asked Shankara which self should move, since it's the same self in both, and Shankara bowed.
tie.friend: Priya can tell Sam that Nani's namaste to the plumber is the same bow she gives the pandit: one self in every body.
tie.you: who do you look past without really seeing?

purusha.meaning: the person, the one who dwells in the city

atman.meaning: the self, the real you, seated within

Shankara.meaning: a great Hindu teacher, traditionally of the 8th century, of Advaita (non-dual) Vedanta

namaste.meaning: a greeting with folded hands: I bow to you

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 5.13 (the city of nine gates)
Shvetashvatara Upanishad 3.18; Katha Upanishad 2.2.1 (the body as a city with gates); Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.5.18 (purusha as the one dwelling in every city)
The chandala episode at Varanasi, traditionally framing the Manisha Panchakam (attributed to Shankara); also told in Madhava-Vidyaranya's Shankara-digvijaya
